title: The Average That Hid Two Stories

scenario.situation: A pricing experiment concluded last week. The average revenue-per-user difference between treatment and control is essentially zero (+0.3%, p=0.71), so the team has filed it as a neutral result and is preparing to roll back.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The product team concludes the pricing change had no impact and plans to deprioritize pricing work entirely this quarter.
scenario.question: Is the null result real, or is something hiding inside the average?

decisions.prompt: The team is ready to move on. How do you frame your investigation before signing off?

options.label: Recheck the p-value with a larger sample
options.detail: Request an extended run of the experiment to get more statistical power on the aggregate metric.
options.consequence: You get a longer run and the aggregate effect is still near zero. More power on the wrong question just gives you a more precise answer to the wrong question.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the aggregate metric and wasted time gaining precision on a misleading summary.

options.label: Diagnostic segmentation of the treatment effect
options.detail: Before accepting the null, slice the treatment effect across user segments to check whether the average conceals opposing subgroup responses.
options.consequence: You find the aggregate is a graveyard average: a large positive lift in one segment and an equally large negative effect in another are canceling each other out. The null was an artifact of aggregation.

options.label: Survey users about price sensitivity
options.detail: Run a post-experiment survey asking users how they felt about the new pricing.
options.consequence: You collect qualitative sentiment, but it can't be linked back to the revenue signal with confidence. The answer was already in the behavioral data.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow, self-report instrument when the behavioral data already contained the answer.

options.label: Accept the null and write the post-mortem
options.detail: The test was properly powered and the result is clear — document it and move on.
options.consequence: The post-mortem goes out and the rollback happens. Two large business opportunities — targeting high-intent users and protecting price-sensitive ones — are buried under the words 'no effect.'
options.divergenceCost: Accepted a statistically convenient summary without checking whether heterogeneity invalidated it.

decisions.prompt: You decide to segment. The experiment platform gives you a breakdown by user segment. Which cut do you trust to confirm or deny the real story?

artifact.title: Average revenue-per-user change by segment — treatment vs. control (raw $)
artifact.caption: Raw dollar differences look small in aggregate. But is the all-users average the right lens, or does segment size distort the picture?

options.label: Raw revenue-per-user delta across segments
options.detail: Compare the absolute dollar change in revenue-per-user for each segment as reported.
options.consequence: The dollar deltas look moderate and partially offset. Because segment sizes differ, you can't tell whether the +$4.10 and -$3.90 represent similarly large proportional swings or whether one is a small relative blip. The story is still blurry.
options.divergenceCost: Compared absolute dollar deltas across unequally sized segments — segment size differences still confound the magnitude of each effect.

options.label: Relative lift (% change in revenue-per-user) by segment
options.detail: Express each segment's treatment effect as a percentage change from its own control baseline, then compare.
options.consequence: Normalized to each segment's own baseline, the signal is unmistakable: high-intent users saw a +19% lift while price-sensitive users saw a -22% drop — both large and in opposite directions. Casual browsers were genuinely unaffected. The null average was entirely an artifact of two big effects canceling.

artifact.title: Relative lift in revenue-per-user by segment (% vs. own control baseline)
artifact.caption: Relative to each segment's own baseline, two large opposing effects emerge clearly. The aggregate masks both — casual browsers are the only segment truly unaffected.

decisions.prompt: The relative-lift view shows +19% for high-intent users and -22% for price-sensitive users, canceling in aggregate. What do you tell the product team?

options.label: "The null was wrong — roll out to high-intent users now and exclude price-sensitive ones."
options.detail: Declare the heterogeneous effects confirmed and recommend the targeted rollout immediately.
options.consequence: You've made a causal targeting recommendation from a single observational segmentation cut. If the segment labels are noisy or the segments differ on confounders beyond intent, the targeted rollout may not replicate the lift — and could actively harm the price-sensitive group at scale.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped from a correlational segment finding directly to a causal deployment decision.

options.label: "The aggregate masks two large opposing effects — this isn't neutral. We should validate with a targeted experiment before acting."
options.detail: Present the heterogeneous-effects finding as evidence against the null conclusion, and recommend a pre-registered follow-up experiment that explicitly randomizes within identified segments.
options.consequence: The product team now sees a genuinely interesting signal rather than a dead end. You've reframed the experiment's outcome correctly, flagged the inferential gap between a post-hoc segmentation and a causal claim, and given a clear next step — a targeted A/B — to confirm before any rollout decision.

insight: The pricing change wasn't neutral — it produced a +19% lift for high-intent users and a -22% drop for price-sensitive ones, two effects large enough to be commercially significant but arithmetically designed to cancel in the average. The team's mistake wasn't bad statistics; it was stopping at the aggregate. The core lesson: a null average result is a hypothesis about homogeneity, not a finding — always interrogate it with segment-level relative lifts before concluding nothing happened.
